definition: Antithetical means directly opposed or contrasted; being the exact opposite of something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word antithetical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know antithetical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Rushing the decision through in a single afternoon was antithetical to the committee's long tradition of slow, careful review.
Two ideas can be different and still sit comfortably side by side, while antithetical ideas are direct opposites of each other.
Antithetical positions are exact opposites, but irreconcilable ones have hardened so completely that no compromise between them will ever be possible.

Contrary means completely opposed in nature or direction, like a contrary wind that pushes against your course. Antithetical is the stronger, more formal claim: one thing is the exact mirror opposite of another, usually a principle or value. Contrary things push against each other; antithetical things cancel each other out.

Opposed means set against something - a person, plan, or force in active conflict with another - and the opposition can be partial or negotiable. Antithetical says something stricter: the two things are exact opposites in principle, with no overlap possible. You can be mildly opposed to a plan; a plan is antithetical to a value it reverses.

A hiking club wrote one rule into its founding charter: every trip must be open to beginners.
Years later, a faction proposed invitation-only expeditions limited to elite climbers.
Longtime members objected that closed trips were antithetical to the club's founding rule, the exact opposite of the openness it promised.
The proposal failed, because a club built on welcoming newcomers could not adopt a policy dedicated to shutting them out.
The invitation-only policy was the direct opposite of the club's founding principle of openness, which is exactly what antithetical means.

Save it for genuine opposites; for things that are merely different or mildly at odds, choose a weaker word.

The journalism teacher kept one rule taped above the classroom door: print nothing you cannot show a reader how you learned.
So when a student proposed running an article built on an anonymous tip no one could verify, the room went quiet.
It was not merely against the rules, the teacher said; it was antithetical to the paper's whole reason for existing.
A paper that hides its sourcing does not bend the rule about showing your work -- it reverses it.
The story ran two weeks later, after the tip had been confirmed on the record by three named sources.
